title: On the Role of Sulfur for the Selective Electrochemical Reduction of CO2 to Formate on CuSx Catalysts
abstract: The efficient electroreduction of CO2 has received significant attention as it is one of the crucial means to develop a closed-loop anthropogenic carbon cycle. Here, we describe the mechanistic workings of an electrochemically deposited CuSx catalyst that can reduce CO2 to formate with a Faradaic efficiency (FEHCOO) of 75% and geometric current density (jHCOO) of −9.0 mA/cm at −0.9 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode. At this potential, the formation of other CO2 reduction products such as hydrocarbons and CO was notably suppressed (total FE < 4%). The formate intermediate (HCOO*) was identified by operando Raman spectroscopy with isotopic labeling. A combination of electrochemical and materials characterization techniques revealed that the high selectivity toward formate production can be attributed to the effect of S dopants on the Cu catalyst, rather than surface morphology. Density functional theory calculations showed that the presence of sulfur weakens the HCOO* and *COOH adsorption energies, such that the formation of *COOH toward CO is suppressed, while the formation of HCOO* toward formate is favored.

sections.heading: 1. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
The electroreduction of CO2 using renewable electricity is a sustainable way to mitigate global CO2 concentrations and to produce important chemicals.1,2 A key product from the electroreduction of CO2 is formic acid (HCOOH). Formic acid is the anode fuel in the direct formic acid fuel cell and is also an excellent hydrogen carrier with a volumetric capacity of 53 g H2/L.
3,4 Various electrocatalysts have been found to selectively reduce CO2 to formic acid/formate. These are based mainly on metals such as tin, lead, bismuth, and cobalt.1,5−9 However, many of these catalysts suffer from the need of a large overpotential or poor stability in reducing CO2 to appreciable amounts of formic acid. For example, graphenesupported SnO2 nanocrystals required a rather negative potential of approximately −1.2 V versus reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) to reduce CO2 to formate with a Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 94%.6 On the other hand, while a Pd70Pt30/ C alloy can catalyze formate production with an FE of 88% at a low potential of −0.4 V versus RHE, it deactivates after ∼2 h due to CO poisoning.10−12 The scarcity of Pd and Pt metals
also precludes their large-scale application in the industry. For these reasons, there has been a significant impetus to develop a new generation of more scalable, robust, and efficient catalysts to electroreduce CO2 to formic acid. Catalysts prepared from CuSx have been recently discovered to exhibit high FEs for formate production.13−15 This catalytic activity is distinct from that of metallic Cu and its oxides, which tend to favor the formation of CO, hydrocarbons, and alcohols, while showing only ∼20% FE for formate.16−18 Zhu et al. first reported that Cu catalysts prepared from the electroreduction of Cu2S on Cu foam substrates could produce formate with an FE of 85%.13 They proposed that the high selectivity toward formate arose from the surface morphologies of the Cu2S-derived Cu
0 catalyst, which had nanosheetassembled flowerlike patterns. Our group subsequently showed that sulfur-doped Cu electrodes could reduce CO2 to formate

with an FE of 74% and a partial current density of −10.7 mA/ cm2 at −0.8 V versus RHE.14 The total FE for CO, hydrocarbons, and alcohols was less than 2%. A positive correlation was found between the sulfur content of the catalysts and their ability to reduce CO2 to formate. A similarly enhanced production of formate on sulfur-modified Cu electrodes was also reported by Shinagawa et al.15
Based on the above works, a key question remains unanswered: how is the selective reduction of CO2 to formate (HCOO−) on the CuSx promoted? Herein, by comparing the CO2 catalytic performances of active CuSx (AC-CuSx), desulfurized CuSx (DS-CuSx), and bare Cu catalysts, we show that the presence of sulfur is crucial. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations further demonstrate that sulfur’s effect on the binding strengths of HCOO* and *COOH adsorbates is responsible for the selectivity toward formate.

sections.heading: 2. EXPERIMENTAL SECTION
sections.text:
2.1. Catalyst Preparation. All samples were prepared on Cu disc
substrates (10 mm diameter, 99.99%, Goodfellow). The Cu disk surfaces were dominated by (111) phases (Section S1, Supporting Information). A three-electrode setup was used for catalyst electrodeposition. A platinum wire and Ag/AgCl (saturated KCl, Pine) were used as the counter and reference electrodes, respectively. Unless specifically stated, a Gamry 600 potentiostat was used for all electrochemical measurements.
2.1.1. Bare Cu. The Cu disks were mechanically polished using diamond slurries (DiaPro 15 and 3 μm, Struers). They were then sonicated and rinsed with water.
2.1.2. Fresh CuSx. CuSx films were electrochemically deposited onto the polished Cu disks using square wave voltammetry (2000 cycles), with a “forward” potential of −0.54 V versus RHE for 10 ms and a “reverse” potential of 0.21 V for 20 ms (unless specifically stated, all potentials hereafter are referenced to the RHE).19 The plating solution contained 4 mM CuSO4·5H2O (98.5−101%,GCE), 4 mM thiourea (≥99.0%, Sigma-Aldrich), and 0.648 M HCl (37%, RCI Labscan).
2.1.3. Active CuSx (AC-CuSx). The fresh CuSx samples were reduced in 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte (99.7%, Merck) at −0.85 V for 5 min before their use as catalysts for CO2 reduction in fresh electrolytes.
2.1.4. Desulfurized CuSx (DS-CuSx). Desulfurized CuSx was prepared by reducing a freshly prepared CuSx catalyst at −1000 mA/cm2 for 30 min in 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte (Metrohm Autolab PGSTAT30). The 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte was replaced every 10 min with a fresh solution.
2.2. Materials Characterization. The physical and elemental compositions of the catalysts were examined using X-ray diffraction (XRD, Panalytical X’Pert PRO high-resolution XRD and Bruker D8 Advance), scanning electron microscopy (SEM, JEOL JSM-6701F), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and energy-dispersive Xray (EDX) spectroscopy (JEOL JEM-3011). TEM samples were prepared by removing the catalyst films from the substrates and dispersing them in ethanol. The suspensions were then drop-casted onto TEM grids (LC325-Ni, 300 mesh, Electron Microscopy Sciences). The electronic structures of the samples were examined
DOI: 10.1021/acsami.8b08428 ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
B
by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) in Kratos AXIS UltraDLD (Kratos Analytical Ltd., chamber pressure 5 × 10−9 Torr) using Al Kα radiation (hν = 1486.71 eV, 5 mA, 15 kV) (Section S2, Supporting Information). The electron binding energies were calibrated against the C1s peak at 285.0 eV. The surfaces of CuSx, AC-CuSx, and DSCuSx were also characterized with cyclic voltammetry (CV) in N2saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte (Section S3, Supporting Information). 2.3. Electrochemical Reduction of CO2 and CO. CO2/CO reduction was performed in a two-compartment Teflon cell, separated by an anion-exchange membrane (Selemion AMV, AGC Asahi Glass).16,17 Both compartments were bubbled with either 20 cm3/min of CO2 (99.999%, Linde Gas) or 5 cm
3/min of CO gas (99.9%, Air Liquide) during the chronoamperometry (duration: 40 min) measurements. A Ag/AgCl (saturated KCl, Pine) and a Pt wire were, respectively, used as the reference and counter electrodes. The iR drop was compensated through the current interrupt mode. All of the current densities reported in this work were normalized against the exposed geometric surface areas (0.238 cm2) of the working electrodes. The gas products were analyzed by gas chromatography (7890A, Agilent). The hydrocarbons (CH4, C2H4) were detected using a flame ionization detector (FID). CO gas was first converted to methane using a methanizer and then detected by a FID. H2 gas was detected by a thermal conductivity detector. Formate was quantified by highperformance liquid chromatography (1260 Infinity, Agilent) with a variable wavelength detector. The other liquid products were quantified by gas chromatography with a headspace sampler (7890B, Agilent) and a FID detector. 2.4. Operando Raman Spectroscopy. A Teflon dish cell was employed for Raman spectroscopy and electrochemical measurements.20 A Ag/AgCl (saturated KCl) and a Pt wire were, respectively, used as the reference and counter electrodes. The working electrode was sheathed in Teflon and had an exposed area of 0.50 cm2. The electrolytes were (a) 0.1 M KHCO3 in H2O, (b) 10 mM KHCOO (potassium formate) in H2O, (c) 0.1 M KHCO3 with 10 mM HCOOH (98%, Fluka) in H2O, (d) 0.1 M KDCO3 in D2O (99.96 at
% D, Cambridge Isotope Laboratories), (e) 10 mM KDCOO (deuterated potassium formate) in D2O, and (f) 0.1 M KDCO3 with 10 mM DCOOD (95 wt % solution in D2O, 98 at % D, Meryer) in D2O. The 0.1 M KDCO3 electrolyte was prepared by saturating 0.05 M K2CO3 (99%, GCE) in D2O solution with CO2 gas (CO2 + D2O + K2CO3 → 2KDCO3). The 10 mM KHCOO in H2O and KDCOO in D2O electrolytes were prepared, respectively, by neutralizing HCOOH with KOH (99.99%, Sigma-Aldrich) and neutralizing DCOOD with KOD (40 wt % solution in D2O, 98 at % D, SigmaAldrich).
Raman spectroscopy was performed using a Raman microscope (Horiba Jobin Yvon). A He−Ne laser (632.8 nm, CVI Melles Griot) served as the excitation source. An air objective (Olympus MPlan N, numerical aperture 0.75) was used for analyzing samples in air, whereas a water immersion objective (Olympus LUMFL, numerical aperture 1.10) was used for operando measurements during electrolysis. The schematic diagram of the Raman setup is available in our previous publication.20
2.5. Computational Method. The reaction pathways for the formation of formate and CO were investigated using density functional theory (DFT) calculations. The bare copper surface model was constructed using a Cu(111) facet (4 × 4 supercells). To represent the surface of the AC-CuSx sample, we substitute one surface copper atom in the 4 × 4 supercell with one sulfur atom. This model was termed CuS1. The free energy diagrams of the electrochemical steps on the two surfaces were constructed according to the method of Nørskov and co-workers21 and calculated as referenced to RHE. Details of the calculations are provided in Sections S4.1 and S4.2, Supporting Information.

sections.heading: 3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
sections.text:
3.1. SEM, TEM, XPS, XRD, and Electrochemical Characterizations of the Catalysts. Freshly prepared CuSx films consisted of nanowires and nanoparticles, as shown by the SEM and TEM analyses (Figure 1a-i,b-i). TEM-EDX and XPS measurements revealed that they
DOI: 10.1021/acsami.8b08428 ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
C
contained 5.8−6.9 at % sulfur (Figure 1c-i and Section S2, Supporting Information). The electron binding energies of the S 2p peaks were at 162.1/163.3 eV, which could be assigned to S2− species.22,23 S2
2− (disulfides) peaks expected at 163.7/ 164.9 eV were not observed.23 XRD analysis further identified the presence of Cu2S and Cu2O (Section S1, Supporting Information). The CuSx films were then subjected to 5 min prereduction at −0.85 V in 0.1 M KHCO3 before being used as catalysts (which we termed as AC-CuSx) for CO2 reduction. The morphology of AC-CuSx was that of corrugated nanowires and nanoparticles (Figure 1a-ii,b-ii), and its sulfur content was reduced to 1.0−1.1 at % (Figure 1c-ii and Section S2, Supporting Information). The stability of AC-CuSx was also monitored after 40 min of CO2 reduction at a representative potential of −0.85 V. Its morphology (Figure 1a-iii,b-iii) and sulfur content (0.8−1.0 at %, Figure 1c-iii and Section S2, Supporting Information) remained almost unchanged. The binding energy of the S 2p peaks also remained the same. A desulfurized sample (termed DS-CuSx) was also prepared by reducing fresh CuSx at −1000 mA/cm2 for 30 min. SEM and TEM images of DS-CuSx showed that its morphology is similar to that of AC-CuSx (Figure 1a-iv,b-iv). Sulfur was not detected (Figure 1c-iv and Section S2, Supporting Information). Cyclic voltammetry was used to examine these surfaces in
N2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte (Section S3, Supporting Information). In the CV of fresh CuSx, a cathodic peak at ca. −0.45 V and an anodic peak at ca. −0.1 V were observed. These have been respectively attributed to Cu2S reduction (Cu2S + H2O + 2e
− → 2Cu + HS− + OH−) and its reversed reaction.15,24 However, these peaks could not be discerned in the CVs of AC-CuSx and DS-CuSx. This CV analysis is consistent with the XPS/TEM-EDX results, which showed that a 5 min prereduction of CuSx could remove the majority of sulfur (to give AC-CuSx). Shinagawa et al. have also reported the absence of these peaks on their sulfurmodified copper catalysts after CO2RR.15
3.2. Electrochemical Reduction of CO2 and CO. 3.2.1. Electrochemical Reduction of CO2. The performance of the AC-CuSx catalyst for CO2 reduction was measured at potentials from −0.7 to −1.0 V. The Faradaic efficiencies and current densities of the products obtained are summarized in Figure 2 and Section S5.1, Supporting Information. Formate was produced with an FE of 61.3% at −0.7 V. As the potential increased to −0.85 and −0.9 V, the FE for formate reaches as high as 75%, with partial current densities (jHCOO−) of −5 and −9 mA/cm2, respectively. The jHCOO− in our work is
comparable to those recently reported for SnO2 and Pd70Pt30 catalysts.6,10 A Tafel slope value of 242 mV/dec for formate production was measured (Section S5.2, Supporting Information). The FEs of hydrocarbons, CO, and alcohols were less than 4% at potentials between −0.70 and −0.90 V. These results are distinct from that obtained on a bare Cu sample, which showed 22.5% FE for formate at a reaction potential of −0.85 V, while the total FE of CO, hydrocarbons, and other liquid products was 9% (Table 1). Considering that sulfur is still present on the surface after
CO2 reduction, we propose that it is associated with the high selectivity toward formate production. In support of this, we found that on DS-CuSx surface with no detectable S content, CO2 reduced to formate with an FE of 29.3% at −0.85 V, while the total FE for CO, hydrocarbons, and other liquid products could reach 27.9%. The hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) was also suppressed on AC-CuSx (FEH2 = 22.2%, jH2= −1.49 mA/cm 2), as compared to that on DS-CuSx (FEH2 = 38.0%, jH2 = −1.85 mA/ cm2) (Table 1). This is verified by comparing their cyclic voltammograms in N2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte, where the HER onset for AC-CuSx was found to occur at a larger overpotential (Section S3, Supporting Information). Considering that AC-CuSx and DS-CuSx samples exhibited similar morphologies but different sulfur contents, we believe that the presence of sulfur (and not morphology) is responsible for the enhanced production of formate and the suppression of H2 and hydrocarbon formation. This proposition is consistent with our earlier work with S-doped Cu, prepared by dipping oxide-derived Cu substrates in ammonium polysulfide solution.14 That catalyst, despite having a completely different morphology (foamlike structure) from the AC-CuSx catalysts reported here, had also exhibited good selectivity for formate production (FE = 74% at −0.80 V). At −0.95 and −1.0 V on the AC-CuSx samples, the FEs for formate decreased significantly to 37.1 and 18.5%, respectively, while the total FE of CO, H2, hydrocarbons, and alcohols increased to 56.4 and 75.0%, respectively (Section S5.1, Supporting Information). This could be ascribed to the loss of sulfur in the form of H2S or HS
− from the AC-CuSx catalysts when such negative potentials were applied.25 The CO2 reduction activities of the films thus resembled that of Cu. We monitored the catalytic performance and surface
composition of AC-CuSx over 3 h of continuous CO2 reduction at −0.85 V (Section S6, Supporting Information). The FE for formate decreased from 76.7 to 71.9% after 3 h of
DOI: 10.1021/acsami.8b08428 ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
D
electrolysis. The morphology of the sample after it was used for CO2 electrolysis was maintained. XPS analysis, however, revealed that the S content lowered from ∼1 (in AC-CuSx, Figure 1c-ii) to 0.4 at %, which could explain the decrease in the sample’s catalytic activity. Herein, we note that the main focus of this work is to study the role of sulfur for selective reduction of CO2 to formate using operando Raman spectroscopy (and density functional theory). The CuSx film was, thus, kept thin to optimize the Raman signals that come from reacting species (instead of the nonactive bulk species). The drawback is that this thin film is not ideal for use in longterm catalysis (durability = 3 h). We refer the reader to our earlier work where a thicker and more robust S-doped Cu film was prepared and was shown to be relatively stable over 12 h of electrolysis.14
3.2.2. Electrochemical Reduction of CO. Next, we seek to understand why the formation of CO and hydrocarbons/ alcohols (whose precursors are CO) was suppressed on ACCuSx catalysts during CO2 reduction. To identify the cause, direct CO reduction was performed on AC-CuSx and DS-CuSx electrodes at −0.85 V (Table 1 and Section S7, Supporting Information). The data for CO reduction on a bare Cu electrode is also included for reference. In contrast with the results obtained from CO2 reduction, CH4, C2H4, and other liquid products apart from formate were obtained on both ACCuSx and DS-CuSx electrodes, with a similar total FE of ∼6% and a partial current density of approximately −0.5 mA/cm2. This finding indicates that the reduction of CO per se was not inhibited by the S adsorbates on the Cu surfaces. We suggest that the S dopants on Cu surfaces had tuned the CO2 reduction pathway toward formate production very early on,
specifically, by suppressing the formation of precursors for CO, such as *COOH, during CO2 reduction. 26
3.3. Raman Spectroscopy. It is known that CO2 could be reduced to a formate intermediate (HCOO*).26,27 The HCOO* could then convert to formate product (HCOO−) through a one-electron transfer from the catalyst. CO2 could also reduce to a carboxyl intermediate (*COOH). The *COOH could then either dehydroxylate to form *CO or react with hydrogen to produce formic acid.26,28 In this section, we apply Raman spectroscopy to identify these intermediates and to probe the evolution of the catalysts during the electrochemical reduction of CO2.
3.3.1. Operando Raman Spectroscopy during CO2 Electroreduction. Bare Cu, AC-CuSx, and DS-CuSx electrodes were first characterized in ambient environment by Raman spectroscopy (Figure 3a). Two bands at 525 and 625 cm−1, which can be assigned to Cu2O, were observed on all the three surfaces.29−31 The formation of Cu2O can be attributed to Cu being oxidized when it came in contact with air.32 The Cu−S stretching vibration [ν(Cu−S)] at 295 cm−1 was only detected on AC-CuSx but not on DS-CuSx,
33,34 consistent with the XPS and EDX analyses that the latter sample is sulfur-free (Section 3.1). Additionally, the absence of the S−S stretching band [ν(S−S)] at ∼470 cm−1 on AC-CuSx agrees with the XPS measurements that the S atoms therein were in the monosulfide (S2−) form.33,34
Operando Raman spectroscopy was performed on the same samples during chronoamperometry at −0.45, −0.65, and −0.80 V in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte (Figure 3b−d and Section S8, Supporting Information). We could not extend the Raman measurements to more negative potentials as the evolution of gas bubbles interfered with the collection of
DOI: 10.1021/acsami.8b08428 ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
E
Raman signals. At −0.45 V, the disappearance of the 525/625 cm−1 bands indicated that Cu2O on the bare Cu surface was reduced to Cu0 (Figure 3b), consistent with predictions using the Cu−H2O Pourbaix diagram and our previous work.17,35 Interestingly, a broad band at 2890 cm−1 started to appear. Its identity will be elucidated in the next section. At −0.65 V, three new peaks were recorded at 275, 356, and 2080 cm−1, which increased in intensity as the potential further changed to −0.80 V. These three peaks can be, respectively, ascribed to CO frustrated rotation, Cu−CO vibration, and CO stretching vibration of *CO intermediates adsorbed on Cu.36,37 CO is a known reaction intermediate of CO2 reduction, and an increase in its band intensities indicates a buildup of *CO intermediates on the bare Cu surfaces.26
The Cu2O bands on AC-CuSx disappeared during CO2 reduction, while the [ν(Cu−S)] peak persisted at all potentials investigated (Figure 3c). The latter observation confirms the presence of S atoms on the catalyst. The absence of *CO signals indicated that the S dopants suppressed the formation of *CO intermediates, in agreement with the low Faradaic efficiencies of CO and ethylene detected on the same surface (Section 3.2). We note that the 2890 cm−1 peak was absent. The Raman spectra of DS-CuSx are similar to those of bare Cu electrodes (Figure 3d and Section S9, Supporting Information), which is expected since all of the S atoms had been removed from its surface. We acknowledge that a trace amount of subsurface oxygen,
which cannot be detected by Raman spectroscopy, might be present in all of the Cu catalysts even if these were biased at negative potentials.38 However, these O atoms (if present) are known to aid in the formation of C2 products, rather than formate.38,39
3.3.2. Identification of 2890 cm−1 Raman Band. We shall now elucidate the identity of the 2890 cm−1 band (Figure 4
and Section S10, Supporting Information). The Raman spectrum of bare Cu was first measured at −0.45 V in N2saturated KHCO3 electrolyte (spectrum 1 in Figure 4). The spectrum was featureless, except for a broad H2O band at ∼3300 cm−1.40 The absence of the 2890 cm−1 peak in N2saturated electrolyte indicated that this peak is related to CO2 reduction intermediates or products, possibly formate.37
Raman spectra collected in 10 mM KHCOO (in H2O) and 0.1 M KHCO3/10 mM HCOOH electrolytes at −0.45 V exhibited the same 2890 cm−1 peak (spectra 2 and 3), which further showed that the peak was due to formate and not bicarbonate. A Raman spectrum of Cu in CO2-saturated KHCO3 electrolyte was also measured and shown for reference (spectrum 4). This 2890 cm−1 peak could be from the C−H stretching vibration [ν(C−H)] of adsorbed formate.41,42 To assess its identity, Raman spectra of the Cu disc in completely deuterated electrolytes (10 mM KDCOO in D2O, N2saturated 0.1 M KDCO3/10 mM DCOOD mixture, and CO2-saturated 0.1 M KDCO3) were recorded (spectra 5−7). Here, a new band appeared at ∼2140 cm−1, along with a weakened 2890 cm−1 band. The decrease in frequency from ∼2890 to ∼2140 cm−1 agrees with an isotopic shift factor of ∼0.74 predicted using the harmonic oscillator model for ν(C− D)/ν(C−H).40 The peak at ∼2140 cm−1 can thus be attributed to the ν(C−D) vibration of chemisorbed DCOO−.40,42
It is notable that the 2890 cm−1 band persisted in the deuterated electrolytes, which indicates that it consisted of more than one vibrational mode. A similarly broad band at ∼2885 cm−1 from chemisorbed DCOO− on aluminum oxide using inelastic electron tunneling spectroscopy has been previously shown.42 Hyens has also reported a 2978 cm−1 Raman peak for the Cu(DCOO)2 salt. 43 We propose that the C−O symmetric (expected at ∼1350 cm−1) and asymmetric stretching (∼1560 cm−1) vibrations of formate could combine to form a new band at ∼2890 cm−1.44 This peak can be regarded as a marker for adsorbed formate, especially at a nonhydrocarbon-producing potential of −0.45 V on bare Cu catalysts, where no interference from the ν(C−H) bands of hydrocarbons is expected (Section S5.3, Supporting Information). The vibrational frequencies of HCOO* and DCOO*
adsorbed on Cu(111) were calculated using DFT (Section S4.3, Supporting Information). The simulated ν(C−H) and ν(C−D) frequencies were, respectively, at ∼2960 and ∼2180 cm−1. These results corroborate our previous assignment of the 2890 and 2140 cm−1 bands. The symmetric and asymmetric stretching vibrational frequencies of C−O were, respectively, calculated to be ∼1305 and ∼1525 cm−1. The HCOO* intermediates probed on bare Cu and DSCuSx surfaces are thus likely precursors to HCOO −. The absence of its signals on AC-CuSx could be attributed to its faster turnover frequency (high jHCOO−) on this surface, as compared to that on DS-CuSx and bare Cu. No signals belonging to *COOH intermediates were detected.
3.4. Effects of Sulfur on the Reaction Pathways for the Production of Formate and CO. Herein, we apply DFT calculations to predict the effects of sulfur on the reaction pathways toward formate and CO production and the H2 evolution reaction on Cu(111) and CuS1 surfaces.
3.4.1. Formate Production Pathway via HCOO* Intermediate. The Gibbs free energies of the dominant pathways
DOI: 10.1021/acsami.8b08428 ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
F
for formate production on Cu(111) and CuS1 surfaces via HCOO* intermediates at different potentials are presented in Figure 5a−c.45 At 0 V and at a low HCOO* coverage of 0.063 ML (Figure 5a), the second proton−electron transfer is the potential-limiting step for formate production on both surfaces. CuS1 shows higher free energy uphill by 0.11 eV than Cu(111). This is because at a low coverage of 0.063 ML, HCOO* adsorbs stronger on CuS1 (−3.15 eV) than on Cu(111) (−2.97 eV). The experimental onset potential observed for formate production on AC-CuSx and bare Cu was at −0.45 and −0.65 V, respectively (Section S5.3, Supporting Information). The free energy diagrams were thus constructed at −0.45 and −0.65 V with a higher HCOO* coverage of 0.375 ML (a higher coverage would occur when the potential is more negative). Figure 5b indicates that the second proton−electron transfer becomes favorable on CuS1 showing free energy downhill of −0.07 eV, while it is still unfavorable on Cu(111) showing free energy uphill of 0.10 eV. This is due to the weaker HCOO* adsorption on CuS1 (−2.78 eV) than on Cu(111) (−2.89 eV). This result agrees with the experimental observation that CuS1 exhibited a lower onset potential for formate production compared to bare Cu. We attribute this to the effect of the sulfur dopant, which weakens the adsorption of HCOO* to a higher degree when its coverage increases (Section S4.2, Supporting Information). Consequently, the lower onset potential of formate formation on CuS1 could lead to the enhanced formate production observed experimentally on S-doped Cu surface as compared to bare Cu (Section 3.2). At −0.65 V, formate production via HCOO* intermediates is energetically downhill on both surfaces (Figure 5c).
3.4.2. CO Production Pathway via *COOH Intermediate. The free energies of the reaction mechanism for CO formation via *COOH intermediates at 0, −0.45, and −0.65 V on Cu(111) and CuS1, with the last desorption step from *CO to CO(g) being a nonelectrochemical step, are presented in Figure 5d−f.46 At 0 V, the formation of *COOH intermediates is the potential-limiting step for CO production on both surfaces (Figure 5d), consistent with previous works by Nørskov et al.28,45,47 The free energies of the *COOH formation step are more uphill on Cu(111) than on CuS1 by 0.02 eV due to the slightly weaker *COOH adsorption energy on Cu(111) (−1.97 eV) than on CuS1 (−2.14 eV) at a low coverage of 0.063 ML. Similar to the case of HCOO* adsorption, when the coverage of *COOH increases, the S dopants assist significantly in the weakening of *COOH adsorption. At a high coverage of 0.375 ML, the adsorption energy of *COOH becomes weaker on CuS1 (−1.82 eV) than on Cu(111) (−1.89 eV) (Section S4.2, Supporting Information). Consequently, at a *COOH coverage of 0.375 ML and at −0.45 V, the *COOH formation step is more thermodynamically downhill on Cu(111) than on CuS1 by 0.22 eV (Figure 5e). This results in the less favorable formation of *COOH on CuS1 compared to that on Cu(111). Similarly, at more negative potentials of −0.65 and −0.75 V, the formation of *COOH is less thermodynamically favorable on CuS1 than on Cu(111) (Figure 5f and Section S4.4, Supporting Information). It is notable that while the formation of HCOO* is more favorable on Cu(111) than on CuS1 at −0.65 V (Figure 5c), the surface of Cu(111) could possibly be more occupied by

COOH* since CO production on Cu(111) is already favorable at −0.45 V (Figure 5e). Thus, more CO production occurs on Cu(111) than on CuS1. Our calculations have demonstrated that overall at negative
potentials, CuS1 is less favorable toward CO production and more favorable toward formate production. Both effects would lead to the suppressed production of CO and more formate production on AC-CuSx compared to bare Cu surface. We note that the HCOO* or *COOH coverages used in the calculations may not represent the exact equilibrium coverage values on Cu(111) and CuS1, but the effect of sulfur on their adsorption strengths is evident. We also investigate the possibility for forming formate via
the *COOH pathway (Section S4.5, Supporting Information). This pathway was found more exergonic (downhill) toward CO production (Figure 5d−f) as compared to formate production on both Cu(111) and CuS1 surfaces. Thus, the *COOH pathway would be dominant toward the formation of CO rather than formate. The calculated HER limiting potentials are −0.16 and −0.20
V at 0.063 ML of H* on Cu(111) and CuS1, respectively (Section S4.7, Supporting Information). The higher overpotential required for HER on CuS1 will result in the surface exhibiting a delayed onset for H2 evolution, which agrees with the voltammetry results described in Section 3.2. 3.4.3. Stabilities of HCOO*, *COOH, CO*, and H*
Intermediates. Bader charge analysis was employed to probe the effect of surface sulfur atoms on the adsorption strengths of HCOO* and *COOH (Section S4.6, Supporting Information). A high coverage of HCOO* or *COOH drives these intermediates to occupy Cu sites surrounding the sulfur atom, which results in less electron transfer from those Cu sites to the adsorbed HCOO* or *COOH. By increasing the amount of sulfur dopant, HCOO* is expected to be adsorbed weaker. The weaker adsorption of HCOO* would favor the energy downhill of the potential-limiting step for formate production (Figure 5b) and hence enhance its formation. These predictions agree with our previous experimental observation that the sulfur content on the Cu electrode positively correlates with the production of formate.14
The adsorption strengths of *CO and H* intermediates were also estimated (Section S4.2, Supporting Information). CO* adsorbs on Cu(111) and CuS1 with comparable strengths. This is probably because less repulsive dipole− dipole interaction is expected between small *CO adsorbates than in the case of the bigger HCOO* and *COOH adsorbates. This finding suggests that sulfur does not significantly affect the adsorption of *CO on copper surfaces, which explains well the similar CO reduction current densities exhibited by AC-CuSx and DS-CuSx (Table 1). Our study has demonstrated that sulfur dopants, rather than
the surface morphology, are crucial for tuning the reduction of CO2 toward formate on a Cu catalyst. Operando Raman spectroscopy clearly showed that S remained on the AC-CuSx surface during CO2 electrolysis. The shift of reaction pathways toward formate production was confirmed using DFT and is attributed to the sulfur adsorbates modifying the adsorption strengths of HCOO* and *COOH. This work provides a new drive to use p-block dopants to tune the selectivity of electrocatalysts for CO2 electroreduction.

sections.heading: 4. CONCLUSIONS
sections.text:
In summary, this work provides experimental and theoretical insights into how sulfur-doped Cu catalyzes the electroreduction of CO2 to formate. We have prepared a AC-CuSx catalyst, which showed a high selectivity and activity toward formate production (FEHCOO− = 75% and jHCOO− = −9.0 mA/ cm2 at −0.9 V). Sulfur dopants were found to be the determining factor for the enhanced production of formate on the AC-CuSx catalysts. Operando Raman spectroscopy revealed that S dopants remained on the catalyst and suppressed the formation of CO intermediates during CO2 reduction, which explained the decreased FE for the formation of CO, hydrocarbons, and alcohols. DFT calculations corroborated the assignment of the Raman bands. They further suggested that the presence of sulfur on the copper surface modified the adsorption strengths of adsorbed HCOO*, which helped promote the production of formate, while the formation of *COOH, the intermediate to CO, was suppressed.
